e.etymology: A y spelling of Silas. Silas is Paul's companion in the New Testament, and the name is usually taken as a short form of Silvanus, from Latin silva, forest.

assoc.t: Sylas, a champion in the game League of Legends

e.etymology: A short form of Katherine in use since the Middle Ages and long given as a full name. Katherine comes from Greek Aikaterine, of uncertain root, long linked to katharos, pure.
namesakes: Kate Middleton (Catherine, Princess of Wales)
Kate Winslet (actress, Titanic)
Kate Hudson (actress)

assoc.t: Kate Middleton, Princess of Wales
Kate Spade, handbag and fashion brand

e.etymology: A spelling of Marley, an English surname from several places named with Old English leah, a woodland clearing.
namesakes: Marlee Matlin (Oscar-winning actress, Children of a Lesser God and CODA)

e.etymology: From the gemstone, October's birthstone, whose name goes back to Sanskrit upala, jewel. It arrived with the other gem names that came into fashion in the late Victorian era.
namesakes: Opal Lee (activist known as the grandmother of Juneteenth)

assoc.t: opal, the iridescent gem and October birthstone

e.etymology: A double-d spelling of Madison, more common in Britain and Australia. The surname means son of Madde, a medieval pet form of Maud or Magdalene; the 1984 film Splash launched it for girls.
The Spanish form of Thaddeus, from Latin Thaddaeus and Aramaic Taddai, whose meaning is uncertain (often given as heart). Thaddaeus, also called Jude, is one of the twelve apostles.
From Latin amanda, she who is to be loved, the feminine of the saint's name Amandus. It entered regular English use through 18th-century literature and was a top US name in the 1980s.
namesakes: Amanda Seyfried (actress, Mamma Mia!)
Amanda Gorman (inaugural poet)
Amanda Bynes (actress)

e.etymology: Popularized by singer Miley Cyrus, who was born Destiny Hope and nicknamed Smiley, then Miley, as a baby. It entered the US top 1,000 in 2007. Miley also exists as a surname.
namesakes: Miley Cyrus (pop singer and Hannah Montana star)

assoc.t: Miley Cyrus, pop singer and Hannah Montana star

e.etymology: From the Swahili word imani, faith or belief, borrowed from Arabic iman. Imani is the seventh principle of Kwanzaa, which carried it into African American families.

assoc.t: Imani (faith), the seventh principle of Kwanzaa

e.meaning: from Troyes; linked to the ancient city of Troy
e.etymology: From an English surname for someone from Troyes in France. As a first name it is now tied to Troy, the ancient city besieged in Homer's Iliad.
namesakes: Troy Aikman (Hall of Fame Dallas Cowboys quarterback)
Troy Bolton (Zac Efron's character in High School Musical)
Troy Polamalu (Hall of Fame Pittsburgh Steelers safety)

assoc.t: Troy, ancient city of the Trojan War
Troy, 2004 epic film starring Brad Pitt
Troy, Michigan and Troy, New York

e.etymology: A form of Reuben, from Hebrew Re'uven, behold, a son. In Genesis Reuben is Jacob's firstborn. Rubén is the standard Spanish form.
namesakes: Ruben Studdard (American Idol winner)
Rubén Blades (salsa singer and actor)

assoc.t: Reuben sandwich of corned beef and sauerkraut

e.meaning: pet form of Emma, Emily or Emmeline
e.etymology: A pet form of Emma, Emily, Emmeline or Amelia, now given as a name in its own right.
namesakes: Emmy Rossum (actress, Shameless)

assoc.t: Emmy Awards, television's top honors

e.etymology: A spelling of Macy, an English surname usually traced to places called Massy in northern France.

assoc.t: Macy's department stores (spelled Macy)

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English dael, valley, plus tun, settlement.

assoc.t: Dalton, the bouncer hero of the movie Road House
Dalton Gang, outlaw brothers of the Old West

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Carson, a Scottish surname of uncertain origin. With the K and y, American parents now give it mostly to girls.
From rio, the Spanish and Portuguese word for river, and the short name of Rio de Janeiro. Rio is also a separate Japanese girls' name written with various kanji.

assoc.t: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
Rio, 2011 animated film about a blue macaw
Rio, Duran Duran's 1982 hit song and album

e.etymology: A modern American variation on the Biblical name Josiah, with the Ja- of Jason and Jace.
A modern elaboration of Ava with the -ianna ending of names like Arianna and Brianna.
From the English word heaven, in use as a given name since the late 20th century. It also inspired Nevaeh, heaven spelled backward.

e.meaning: peace (the first element of the name is uncertain)
e.etymology: The usual American spelling of Geoffrey, a Norman French name of Germanic origin. Its second element means peace; the first is disputed, and the name was long confused with Godfrey.
namesakes: Jeffrey Wright (actor, Westworld and American Fiction)
Jeffrey Dean Morgan (actor, The Walking Dead)
e.note: Two of the most recognized bearers are infamous: serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

e.etymology: From Nadya, the Russian pet form of Nadezhda, hope, which reached English through French. A separate Arabic name, Nadiyya, is glossed as tender.
namesakes: Nadia Comaneci (Romanian gymnast who scored the first Olympic perfect 10)

assoc.t: Nadia Comaneci, gymnast with the first Olympic perfect 10

e.etymology: From an English surname, possibly a variant of Brindley, a place name meaning burnt clearing. It caught on in the 2010s alongside Kinley and Brynn.
A Latin American spelling of the French name Arlette, also written Arlet. Well used in Mexico, it has risen quickly among Spanish-speaking American families.
From Zaire, a name for the Congo River and, from 1971 to 1997, for the country now called the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It comes through Portuguese from a Kongo word for river.

assoc.t: Zaire, former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo

e.etymology: A spelling of Myla with a final h. Myla is a modern name in the family of Mila, Mya and Kyla.

e.meaning: fallow land (English) or a short form of McClelland (Irish)
e.etymology: From a surname with two sources: an English one for someone living by fallow land, and a shortening of McLeland or McClellan, Irish for son of the servant of Saint Faolán.
namesakes: Leland Stanford (railroad magnate who founded Stanford University)
Leland Palmer (Laura's father on Twin Peaks)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jonathan shaped by the unrelated name John. Jonathan is Hebrew Yehonatan, Yahweh has given; in the Bible he is King Saul's son and David's loyal friend.
The French feminine form of Daniel, from Hebrew for God is my judge. Its American peak came in 1987, when it ranked in the top 20.
namesakes: Danielle Steel (best-selling romance novelist)
Danielle Fishel (Topanga on Boy Meets World)

e.etymology: A modern American name that puts a K on the pattern of Aaliyah; also spelled Kaliya and Kaleah.

e.meaning: pet form of Alice, Alison, Alexandra and other Al- names
e.etymology: A pet form of Alice, Alison, Alexandra and other names beginning with Al-. In the 19th century it was given to both girls and boys; today it is almost all girls.
namesakes: Allie Hamilton (Rachel McAdams's character in The Notebook)

e.etymology: A spelling of Blair, a Scottish surname from places named with Gaelic blàr, plain or field, often a battlefield. The final e is an American touch for girls.

assoc.t: Blair Waldorf, queen bee of Gossip Girl (spelled Blair)

e.meaning: brave with the spear, or spear ruler
e.etymology: From a surname that began as a medieval English and Irish form of Gerard and Gerald, Germanic names that join ger, spear, with words for brave and for rule.
namesakes: Garrett Morris (comedian, original Saturday Night Live cast member)
